title: Drive a piston into its bore through a ring compressor while the other hand holds the compressor flat on the deck
instruction: Install the piston in the bore.
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (about 800,000 US jobs, BLS) and small-engine mechanics fit pistons this way in every engine rebuild, a standard job in engine repair. The rings stand out past the piston, so a ring compressor squeezes them into their grooves and the piston is driven out of the compressor into the bore. Engine manuals and rebuild guides give the rule: hold the compressor down flat and square on the deck while driving the piston, because each ring pushes the band up as it is squeezed past the band's lip, and a band that rides up more than about a millimeter lets that ring spring out, where it can catch on the deck's edge and jam the piston, or break if it is driven on. One hand therefore holds the compressor down the whole time while the other drives the piston home, then both let go.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Engine: a single-cylinder GX200-class short block (68 mm bore, 54 mm stroke, 84 mm rod), head off, held in a steel fixture on the table with its bore vertical, centered at x 26, y -17. Its gray cast crankcase (15 x 17 cm, 11.5 cm tall) stands on the fixture's 20 x 24 cm base plate, with the crankshaft's 19 mm end sticking out toward the robot's right 6 cm above the table, on the crank's axis. Above it the finned cylinder barrel rises to a 13 x 13 cm deck flange whose machined deck, with four head-bolt holes, is 19.75 cm above the table. The bore (a steel liner with a 1 mm chamfer at its mouth) is vertical, axis at x 26, y -17. The crank is turned 44 degrees past top dead center. Piston: aluminum, 67.6 mm across and 5 cm tall, an arrow on the crown, on its connecting rod (piston, pin and rod 250 g); three rings in grooves 5 mm (top compression ring), 9 mm (second ring) and 13 mm (oil ring) below the crown. The rod hangs on its pin with its cap off and is not attached to the crank. The piston starts with its skirt in the bore and its crown 2.2 cm above the deck, with the rod's big end 3.2 cm above the crank journal. It slides only along the bore's axis and seats with the crown 10.2 mm below the deck, where the big end lands on the journal. Ring compressor: pliers type, 200 g, a spring-steel band 1.8 cm tall (68.4 mm inside, rolled lip to 8 cm across) squeezing all three rings, standing on the deck around the piston; its two steel handles, locked squeezed by a ratchet bar and with red vinyl grips on their outer 9 cm, reach from 4 to 19 cm out from the bore's axis toward the robot's left, 20 degrees back from the y axis (ends near x 19.5, y 0.9), 0.8 cm above the deck. The compressor slides only along the bore's axis; nothing holds it down but its weight. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0. Ring escape (0, irreversible, checked over the whole run): a ring that springs out between the band and the deck can catch on the deck's edge and jam the piston, or break if it is driven on, and pressing the band back down doesn't put it back. The sim models the rings' push on the band rather than the ring itself, so escape is a proxy: a ring is crossing while it is within 2.5 mm above the deck (the band's 1.5 mm lower lip plus the bore's 1 mm chamfer), and it escapes when its path during a step passes through the gap under the band while the band is more than 1 mm off the deck (a 1.2 mm-tall top ring fits through a gap over 1 mm), or when the piston is pulled up until a ring's middle is past the band's top edge, where it springs open. The path between steps is checked, so a fast stroke can't skip the gap, and a fast stroke with the band held flat is not an escape. A real trial checks the outcome: a 1 mm feeler gauge or dial indicator at the band's edge on the handle side shows any lift (or film it from the side), and after the run a look into the bore shows any ring caught on the deck's edge, protruding or broken. 1.0: all three rings in the bore (each 1 mm or more below the deck, past the chamfer, so wholly inside the bore), the crown within 2 mm of its seat (half the 4 mm between ring grooves; it can go no lower, since the rod's big end stops on the journal), the compressor resting on the deck within 1 mm, and both hands let go: no gripper touching the piston, the band or its handles. Contact is judged by the gripper's own shape (palm and fingers, fitted to the YAM's collision meshes, at their present opening) coming within 2 mm of a part, the solver's resting gap plus the fit, so a hand hovering near the work has let go. The job ends with the compressor standing free for the mechanic to unlock and lift off, and only then is it known that the band sits flat on its own. The rod's big end is then on the journal, ready for its cap. Otherwise 0.2 for each ring in cleanly (0.2, 0.4 or 0.6): each is a ring through the hard step without escaping that the mechanic doesn't have to redo, but the piston isn't home, so the rod cap can't go on yet, or a hand is still on the work. A credited ring is wholly in the bore and stays in when the hand lets go; a ring still crossing under a band held flat is not credited. Possible scores: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0. Arm positions are not scored. A real trial measures the crown below the deck with a depth gauge and the band's seat with the 1 mm feeler gauge.
reset_notes: Pull the piston back up until its crown is 2.2 cm above the deck, check the three rings are whole and in their grooves (replace a broken ring), close the compressor around them and lock its handles, stand it flat on the deck with the handles pointing as described, and check the crank is still 44 degrees past top dead center (a degree wheel on the crank's end).
fidelity: A shop taps the crown with a hammer handle; here one hand pushes it down steadily. Piston and rod are one slide on the bore's axis; the rod's swing onto the journal isn't modeled, the journal is a stop at the seat. The compressor only slides on that axis, so tipping is modeled as lifting (the 1 mm limit holds for its whole rim). Ring forces are modeled: each crossing ring pushes the piston back with 4 N and the band up with 6 N, falling off at 600 N/m, so an unheld band rides up about 7 mm.
